questions.q: Administrative Law primarily governs:
o: Only criminal proceedings
The organisation, powers, duties, and functions of administrative authorities, and remedies available against their action
Only international treaties
Only private contract disputes
questions.src: Administrative Law addresses the relationship between citizens and administrative/executive authorities and the control mechanisms over administrative power.

questions.q: In Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955), the Supreme Court held that India follows:
o: A rigid, strict separation of powers exactly like the United States
A FUNCTIONAL, not rigid, separation of powers, permitting some overlap between branches
No separation of powers whatsoever
Separation of powers only at the state level, not the Union level
questions.src: Ram Jawaya Kapur confirmed India's functional approach to separation of powers, acknowledging necessary overlap in modern governance.

questions.q: "Delegated Legislation" refers to law-making power:
o: Exercised exclusively by the judiciary
Exercised by the executive (or another subordinate authority) under powers conferred by a parent/enabling statute
That requires no statutory authorisation whatsoever
Exercised only by foreign governments
questions.src: Delegated (subordinate) legislation is executive rule-making under authority granted by the legislature through an enabling Act.

questions.q: In In Re Delhi Laws Act (1951), the Supreme Court held that the legislature:
o: Can delegate absolutely any legislative power without limit
Can delegate ancillary/subordinate matters, but CANNOT delegate its "essential legislative functions" (determining policy)
Cannot delegate any legislative power under any circumstances
Can only delegate power to the judiciary, never the executive
questions.src: This case established the foundational excessive-delegation doctrine — essential legislative functions (policy determination) cannot be delegated, unlike ancillary implementation matters.

questions.q: In Re Delhi Laws Act (1951) was significant procedurally because it was:
o: A routine civil appeal
The FIRST Presidential Reference under Article 143 of the Constitution
A criminal trial
A dispute between two state governments
questions.src: This was the first-ever use of the Article 143 Presidential Reference mechanism, decided by a 7-judge bench.

questions.q: "Excessive Delegation" occurs when the parent statute delegates legislative power:
o: With clear, sufficient policy guidance for the delegate
WITHOUT providing adequate guidance/policy guidelines constraining the delegate's discretion
To a court of law
Only for a specified short duration
questions.src: Excessive delegation is unconstitutional precisely because it lacks the policy guidance needed to keep the delegate's discretion within proper legislative bounds.

questions.q: "Substantive Ultra Vires," as distinguished from "Procedural Ultra Vires," refers to delegated legislation that:
o: Fails to follow a mandatory procedure required by the parent Act
Exceeds the SUBSTANTIVE scope/subject-matter authorised by the parent Act
Is always automatically valid regardless of content
Applies only to criminal matters
questions.src: Substantive ultra vires concerns the CONTENT/scope of the delegated legislation exceeding what was authorised, distinct from procedural defects in HOW it was made.

questions.q: Under the Rule Against Bias (Nemo Judex in Causa Sua), a decision-maker must be free from:
o: Any connection to the case whatsoever, even purely administrative involvement
Personal, financial (pecuniary), or other disqualifying interest that could compromise genuine impartiality
Any prior legal training
Requirements to give reasons for decisions
questions.src: The rule against bias requires genuine impartiality, free from pecuniary, personal, or prejudgment-based disqualifying interests.

questions.q: "Audi Alteram Partem" requires that a person adversely affected by an administrative decision generally receive:
o: No opportunity to respond at all
Proper notice of the case against them and a genuine, reasonable opportunity to be heard/respond
Only a written apology after the decision
The right to appeal to a foreign court
questions.src: Audi alteram partem (hear the other side) requires notice and a genuine opportunity to present one's case before an adverse decision is made.

questions.q: In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the Supreme Court developed the concept of "Post-Decisional Hearing" to address situations where:
o: A hearing is never required under any circumstances
A genuine pre-decisional hearing would frustrate the very purpose of urgent administrative action
The government wishes to avoid all forms of hearing permanently
Only criminal cases are involved
questions.src: Post-decisional hearing is a pragmatic compromise for urgent situations where advance notice would defeat the administrative action's purpose, while still preserving meaningful natural justice.

questions.q: Following Maneka Gandhi, an administrative order can generally be challenged on grounds including:
o: Only if it involves a criminal matter
Being unreasonable, made in bad faith, denying natural justice, or being ultra vires
Only if made by a specific named official
Only within 24 hours of being issued
questions.src: The case established multiple grounds on which administrative orders remain open to legal challenge.

questions.q: Natural justice requirements may generally be EXCLUDED in circumstances such as:
o: Whenever the government simply prefers not to provide a hearing
Genuine emergency situations demanding immediate action, where delay would defeat the purpose entirely
Only for disputes below a certain monetary value
Only on weekends and public holidays
questions.src: Recognised exceptions to natural justice include genuine emergencies and situations where the requirement would be an empty formality causing no real prejudice.

questions.q: Under the classic threefold classification of judicial review grounds, "Irrationality" (Wednesbury Unreasonableness) means a decision:
o: The court simply personally disagrees with
SO unreasonable that no reasonable authority, properly applying its mind, could have arrived at it
That was made too quickly
That involves a large amount of money
questions.src: Wednesbury unreasonableness sets a deliberately high threshold — mere judicial disagreement with a decision is insufficient; the decision must be genuinely irrational.

questions.q: "Procedural Impropriety," as a ground of judicial review, includes:
o: Only errors of substantive law
Failure to follow required procedures, including natural justice violations and non-compliance with mandatory statutory procedures
Only decisions made in a foreign language
Only decisions taken by more than one official
questions.src: Procedural impropriety covers both natural justice failures and non-compliance with statutorily mandated procedures for administrative decision-making.

questions.q: The writ of "Mandamus" is used to:
o: Quash a decision already made by a tribunal
COMPEL a public authority to perform a public duty it has failed or refused to perform
Challenge someone's right to hold public office
Challenge unlawful detention
questions.src: Mandamus ("we command") compels performance of an existing public duty, distinct from the other writs' specific functions.

questions.q: The writ of "Certiorari," as distinguished from "Prohibition," is used to:
o: Prevent a proceeding before it concludes
QUASH a decision ALREADY MADE by a subordinate court/tribunal/authority acting without or in excess of jurisdiction
Compel performance of a duty
Challenge unlawful detention only
questions.src: Certiorari is corrective (quashing a completed decision), while Prohibition is preventive (stopping proceedings before they conclude) — a frequently tested distinction.

questions.q: The writ of "Quo Warranto" challenges:
o: A person's unlawful detention
A person's RIGHT to hold a public office they occupy without proper legal authority/qualification
A tribunal's procedural errors
The validity of a private contract
questions.src: Quo Warranto ("by what authority") specifically questions the legal authority behind someone's occupation of a public office.

questions.q: The traditional requirement of "Locus Standi" (a direct personal legal interest to approach court) has been significantly liberalised in India through:
o: Complete abolition of all standing requirements
Public Interest Litigation (PIL), allowing concerned citizens/organisations to litigate on behalf of disadvantaged groups
Requiring even MORE strict personal interest than before
Only allowing government officials to file cases
questions.src: PIL represents a distinctively Indian judicial development significantly expanding access to judicial review beyond traditional standing requirements.

questions.q: Administrative Tribunals are generally established to provide:
o: Slower, more formalistic dispute resolution than ordinary courts
SPEEDIER, more technically-informed, and less formalistic resolution of specialised disputes
No possibility of appeal or judicial review whatsoever
Resolution only of purely criminal matters
questions.src: Tribunals offer specialised, efficient dispute resolution for technical/specific subject matters, while remaining subject to judicial review.

questions.q: The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT), established under the Administrative Tribunals Act 1985, primarily adjudicates disputes relating to:
o: International trade disputes
Recruitment and service conditions of persons in Union public services
Only criminal appeals
Only tax matters
questions.src: CAT specifically handles service-related disputes for Union government employees, illustrating the specialised tribunal model.

questions.q: The traditional doctrine of "Sovereign Immunity" historically shielded the State from tort liability for acts done in exercise of:
o: Any function whatsoever, with no distinction
"Sovereign" functions (e.g., defence, core governmental activity), while permitting liability for "non-sovereign"/commercial functions
Only functions performed outside India
Only functions performed by private contractors
questions.src: Sovereign immunity traditionally distinguished sovereign (immune) from non-sovereign/commercial (liable) governmental functions.

questions.q: Modern Indian judicial trends regarding sovereign immunity have generally:
o: Expanded sovereign immunity to cover all government functions without exception
NARROWED the sovereign/non-sovereign distinction, recognising it is increasingly ill-suited to a modern welfare state's extensive activities
Abolished the concept of the State entirely
Applied only to foreign governments, never the Indian government
questions.src: Courts have progressively eroded rigid sovereign immunity, reflecting the reality that a welfare state performs many functions beyond traditional core sovereign activities.

questions.q: Under Article 299, a government contract is generally enforceable against the government only if:
o: Made verbally by any government employee
EXPRESSED to be made by the President/Governor and EXECUTED by a person duly AUTHORISED for that purpose
Signed by any citizen willing to contract with the government
Made without any formal documentation at all
questions.src: Article 299 imposes specific formal requirements — express attribution to the President/Governor and execution by an authorised person — for enforceable government contracts.

questions.q: A "Henry VIII Clause" in delegated legislation refers to a provision empowering the executive to:
o: Create an entirely new, unrelated statute
MODIFY or even AMEND provisions of the parent Act itself to remove implementation difficulties
Only interpret existing law, never modify it
Delegate power exclusively to foreign authorities
questions.src: Henry VIII Clauses are viewed with particular judicial caution, since they allow the executive to alter the very primary legislation that authorised it, potentially undermining legislative supremacy.

questions.q: The Doctrine of Proportionality, increasingly applied by Indian courts as an additional ground of review, examines whether administrative action:
o: Was taken by the correct department
Went further than genuinely necessary to achieve a legitimate objective, imposing a disproportionate burden relative to the aim pursued
Was published in the Official Gazette
Was taken within office working hours
questions.src: Proportionality assesses whether the means used were excessive relative to the legitimate end sought, an increasingly significant ground of judicial review particularly in Fundamental Rights contexts.
